name: Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools
title: Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools
answer: Student health information is among the most sensitive records a school holds, and a teacher who types a student's diagnosis, medication or injury into a general chat tool has handed that record to a company the school has no agreement with. The safe approach is to describe the need in general terms, so the tool still helps with planning while no private information leaves the school. Where a plan genuinely turns on medical detail, the nurse and the family belong in the conversation rather than the chat box.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: This idea is about keeping student health details out of general AI chat tools. Records kept by a school nurse are generally part of a student's education records under FERPA, as the book describes in Chapter 3, so passing those details to an outside company is a serious step. A teacher who types a diagnosis, a medication or an injury into a general chat tool has shared that record with a company the school has no agreement with. The name removal habit from Chapter 3 exists to prevent exactly this kind of mistake. Physical education and health teachers run into the risk more than most, because their planning often turns on a particular student's body or condition.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not sort this guidance by grade band, so it applies the same way across a school. A PE teacher planning an adapted activity may be tempted to describe one student's condition in detail, and a health teacher may want help answering a student's personal question. In both cases the identifying details and the health details stay out of the tool. The safe approach is to describe the need in general terms, for example asking for activities suited to a student who has limited use of one arm. The answer is just as useful, and nothing private leaves the school. When a plan depends on medical details, the nurse and the family should be part of the conversation.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its support is the reasoning that nurse records generally fall within education records under FERPA, as set out in Chapter 3, and that a general chat tool is a company the school has no agreement with. The chapter presents the risk as a familiar one for PE and health teachers and the general-terms approach as the practical answer. Nothing in the supplied text measures how often the mistake happens or how well the habit works.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about what must never be typed into a general tool: a student's name together with a diagnosis, a medication or an injury. The judgement about whether a detail identifies a student stays with the teacher, and the text's test is whether the description would still be useful with the identifying and health specifics stripped out. Where an adapted plan truly depends on medical detail, that decision moves to the nurse and the family, who should be part of the conversation rather than left out of it. The tool can still help with general activity ideas, but it does not decide what a student needs. This describes practice, not legal advice.
